# On Fragility

A fair reader reaches this point uneasy. The whole system leans on QR codes, and QR codes fail to scan. Cards get dropped, or soaked, or left at camp. A phone dies. It all seems light enough to blow away in the first hard wind, and light is not a word that inspires trust in a record meant to last centuries. The worry deserves a straight answer.

Start with the codes. A card is not only a code. It also prints its value and its field name in plain letters, large enough to read across a table. If a code won't scan, you read the words with your eyes and type them once, and you've lost a minute, not a specimen. The card carries the same fact three ways, as a printed value, as a printed name, and as a code, so no single failure erases it. The redundancy was built in from the start.

The mirror of that worry is the better one to ask about, and it gets less attention because it doesn't announce itself. A code that fails to read is a nuisance you notice. A code that reads when you didn't mean it to is a wrong fact entering the record silently, and no amount of redundancy helps, because redundancy is for recovering what was lost, not for catching what was never true. There is only one place this can happen here: a code belonging to some card other than the one you rotated out, caught in the same frame. The decks are built to make it impossible rather than to detect it afterward, which is why each one carries a blank card inside its covers. Design the false reading out and you needn't go hunting for it.

The redundancies stack from there, and they're cheap. Glance at the photograph before you move on, and a blurred or half-framed shot is caught while it's seconds to fix, not discovered months later at the desk. Bring a companion and let them photograph the same layout, and a lost or dead phone costs you nothing, because the collection is already on a second one. Carry two sets of cards, and a dropped deck is a shrug rather than a ruined day. None of this is clever. It's just cheap insurance, and cheap insurance is exactly the kind worth buying.

And underneath all of it is a floor. The one thing that must survive is the identity, and the identity rides on the number card and the photograph together: who, where, and when, secured in a single frame. Everything else, the whole set of observation cards, is enrichment stacked on that floor. In a downpour, with cold hands and failing light, you can lay down the number card alone, take one picture, and move on, and the collection is safe. You add the rest when you can. You are never left with nothing.

There's a reason this holds, and it's the reason the whole book has been circling: friction. The system asks you to attend to very little. Lay out a few cards, take one picture, tie one knot. When there is little to watch, you watch it well. The old way asked you to read four instruments and fill a dozen fields with a pencil in the rain, and things slipped, because attention is finite and the field spends it fast. Ask for less and the little you ask for gets done right. Fragility and friction turn out to be the same thing seen twice, and lightening the one strengthens against the other.

The method is also less rigid than it looks, which is the other half of not being fragile. Suppose your work needs something the basic decks never anticipated, say a full roll call of the species growing around your plant. Nothing in the method forbids it. You lay out a group of species cards and photograph them, and if one frame won't hold them all, you take several photographs, each its own group. The act is the same act it has always been, photograph the cards, and it adds no new kind of friction. It only asks for more of the one easy thing. A method that grows by repeating its single move, instead of bolting on a special case for every need, is a sturdy method, not a brittle one.

So here is the honest reply to the worry. The system is light because everything heavy was taken out of it, and light is not the same as weak. It fails softly, it doubles for pennies, it bends to what a particular collector needs, and it stands on a floor that always holds. What's left to show is the one part of all this that is genuinely new, and it is the part worth the most.
